title: The Gold Coins game💛
transcript: It is not the strongest player to win the game, but the most active one. The year is 1912 and Frank Marshall is playing with the black pieces. A player so legendary that his legacy survives to this day as the Marshall Gambit is one of the most aggressive lines in the Ruy Lopez. His opponent Stefan Levitsky has just moved the rook to E5, but Frank Marshall plays rook to H6 attacking the queen and forcing it to move. And he decides to start an attack with the beautiful rook takes H3. Now, of course, the rook cannot be taken because knight to F3 would be a royal fork winning the queen and the game. So, Levitsky decides to counter attack the queen with his rook, but this is where Marshall plays a move so majestic, so incredible, and so powerful that to this day most chess players think of it as the best chess move ever played. And that move that forced Levitsky to resign as soon as he saw it on the board is queen to G3. An incredible find. The queen is hanging three different ways. But the threat is obvious. Black is trying to play queen takes H2 checkmate. So, the queen cannot be ignored. If the queen takes, after this knight check, black is going to pick up some material. This pawn is pinned and if you take this way, this is going to be checkmate. So, after the king moves black is going to simplify and now be up a full knight. If this pawn takes, now knight to E2 again forces the king in the corner and rook takes F1 is checkmate. If H takes G3, this is just checkmate in one move. The legend says that when this move was played on the board, all of the players watching the game unfold in real time decided to throw gold coins at the players for how amazed they were by that move. And when asked about it some years later in an interview, Frank Marshall confirmed that is exactly what happened. If you love historical chess, follow me for more.
